citation: Parent Teacher Home Visits. (2021). Evidence summary reporting a 2021 Mathematica Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic quasi-experimental study. https://www.mathematica.org
title: PTHV five non-negotiables for relationship-building home visits
description: The PTHV model specifies five non-negotiable design features: "Visits are voluntary and arranged in advance"; "Teachers are trained and compensated for visits"; "Visits focus on hopes and dreams"; "Educators visit a cross-section of students (not a targeted intervention)"; and "Educators go in pairs and reflect." These features define how the program is implemented as a universal rather than targeted family engagement practice.
requirements: All five non-negotiables must hold for an implementation to count as PTHV
constraints: The model is explicitly not a targeted intervention; educators visit a cross-section of students
target_learners: All students in a school cross-section, grades 1–5 in the evaluated implementation
target_learning_goals: Relationship building between educators and families to improve instruction
examples: Teachers conduct 30–40 minute visits in pairs, focusing on hopes and dreams, and reflect afterward.
key_sources: Parent Teacher Home Visits. (2021). Evidence summary reporting a 2021 Mathematica Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic quasi-experimental study. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/parent-teacher-home-visits-attendance/

citation: Academic Performance — Parent Teacher Home Visits. (2021). Evidence summary. https://www.evidenceforesscp.org
title: Two-visit home visit structure: relationship-building first, academics second
description: PTHV organizes home visits as a two-visit sequence embedded in ongoing communication. The first visit is relationship-building and occurs in the summer or early fall; a second visit later focuses on academics or another relevant issue for the student or family. The page describes it as "a two-visit model, PTHV encourages the first relationship-building visit to occur in the summer or early fall, followed by ongoing communication throughout the year."
requirements: Visits are voluntary and arranged in advance
Teachers are trained and compensated for visits
target_learning_goals: Building teacher-family relationships and improving instruction for the learner
examples: Educators listen, ask questions, and make observations during visits that they take back to their classrooms to improve instruction.

article_title: A Randomized Controlled Evaluation of Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children
citation: Glen Dunlap, Phillip Strain, Janice K. Lee, Jaclyn Joseph, and Nancy Leech. (2018). A Randomized Controlled Evaluation of Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121417724874
title: Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children (PTR-YC): a standardized five-step individualized positive behavior support model
description: PTR-YC is a standardized model of positive behavior support adapted from the PTR model for toddlers and preschoolers with serious challenging behaviors, intended as the most intensive component of a multitiered framework. "PTR-YC is an approach for implementing highly focused PBS interventions for young children who already exhibit patterns of serious challenging behaviors." It proceeds through five steps: teaming and goal setting (one behavior to decrease, one to increase), simple data collection, functional behavioral assessment using Prevent/Teach/Reinforce checklists, a written behavior intervention plan including at least one strategy from each of the three categories, and data-based decision making.
requirements: The BIP must include at least one strategy from each of the Prevent, Teach, and Reinforce categories
Teams first assess whether classroom-wide practices are implemented with integrity before starting the individualized process
Only two behaviors are targeted at a time to enhance focus and fidelity
constraints: The manual is not a substitute for expertise in function-based intervention; providers need initial training and coaching
Teams in segregated settings had difficulty implementing peer-related social skill strategies without typically developing peers
target_learners: preschool-aged and toddler-aged children with severe and persistent challenging behaviors in pre-K, Head Start, and child care classrooms
target_learning_goals: reduce challenging behavior
increase social skills and appropriate engagement
examples: In the RCT, a trained research facilitator coached each classroom team through the five steps, while teachers and classroom staff implemented all interventions themselves
key_sources: Glen Dunlap, Phillip Strain, Janice K. Lee, Jaclyn Joseph, and Nancy Leech. (2018). A Randomized Controlled Evaluation of Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121417724874

article_title: A Randomized Controlled Evaluation of Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children
citation: Glen Dunlap, Phillip Strain, Janice K. Lee, Jaclyn Joseph, and Nancy Leech. (2018). A Randomized Controlled Evaluation of Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121417724874
title: PTR-YC recommends five classroom-wide practices be in place before or alongside individualized intervention
description: Before beginning the individualized PTR-YC process, teams are advised to verify that classroom-wide practices are implemented with integrity, because high-quality classroom practices often reduce or eliminate challenging behavior without intensive individualized intervention. The article enumerates them: "(a) use of a 5:1 ratio of positive to negative or neutral attention; (b) use of clear, predictable schedules that are prominently displayed and taught to all children", plus embedded routines, direct teaching of behavioral expectations in each daily context, and direct teaching of peer-related social skills.
requirements: Classroom-wide practices must be implemented consistently and with a high level of quality before or simultaneous with the individualized PTR-YC process
target_learners: all children in pre-K, Head Start, and early care and education classrooms
target_learning_goals: prevent challenging behavior and promote healthy social-emotional development
examples: The RCT evaluated PTR-YC as the intensive tier after these classroom-wide practices, with teams checking classroom practice integrity before starting the individualized process
key_sources: Glen Dunlap, Phillip Strain, Janice K. Lee, Jaclyn Joseph, and Nancy Leech. (2018). A Randomized Controlled Evaluation of Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121417724874

article_title: A Randomized Controlled Evaluation of Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children
citation: Glen Dunlap, Phillip Strain, Janice K. Lee, Jaclyn Joseph, and Nancy Leech. (2018). A Randomized Controlled Evaluation of Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121417724874
title: Programs adopting PTR-YC should provide providers with initial training and ongoing coaching, since the manual alone does not ensure expertise
description: The authors draw a practice implication from the RCT: although PTR-YC is manualized, successful implementation depended on highly trained facilitators who coached teams until plans were implemented with fidelity. "for programs interested in utilizing PTR-YC, there is a high likelihood that providers will need some initial training/orientation and also coaching." The article also notes anecdotally that teams became more proficient and needed less coaching across multiple cases.
requirements: Access to highly trained challenging behavior experts or facilitators for coaching during plan implementation
constraints: The article reports no systematic data on coaching dosage; the proficiency observation was anecdotal
target_learners: preschool-aged children with severe and persistent challenging behaviors
target_learning_goals: implement function-based behavior intervention plans with fidelity
examples: In the RCT, each classroom had a research facilitator with at least 5 years of experience who attended all team meetings and coached implementation, while teachers delivered the interventions
key_sources: Glen Dunlap, Phillip Strain, Janice K. Lee, Jaclyn Joseph, and Nancy Leech. (2018). A Randomized Controlled Evaluation of Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121417724874

article_title: Congruence in Parent-Teacher Communication: Implications for the Efficacy of CBC for Students with Behavioral Concerns
citation: S. Andrew Garbacz, Susan M. Sheridan, Natalie A. Koziol, Kyongboon Kwon, Shannon R. Holmes. (2015). Congruence in Parent–Teacher Communication: Implications for the Efficacy of CBC for Students With Behavioral Concerns. School Psychology Review, 44(2), 150–168. https://www.nasponline.org/publications/periodicals/spr
title: PTRS-II Communication-to-Other subscale as the congruent-communication measure
description: The study measured each dyad member's perception of communication using the Communication-to-Other subscale of the Parent–Teacher Relationship Scale II, which is "composed of ﬁve items rated on a 5-point Likert scale." Parallel items comprise the parent and teacher scales, with items such as "I tell this teacher (parent) when I am pleased" and "I ask this teacher (parent) for suggestions." Internal consistency was reported as α = .92 for parents and α = .87 for teachers. Dyadic congruence scores were then derived from the two members' responses using a distance formula, with higher scores indicating less congruence.
requirements: Parallel parent and teacher forms completed by both dyad members; responses to the same five items at each time point
constraints: The authors state that full psychometric properties of this measure as used for congruent communication have not been established, and that congruent communication was measured only via self-reports, with no direct or objective measures of communication included
target_learners: Parents and teachers of K–3 children with behavioral concerns
target_learning_goals: Assessment of parent–teacher communication perceptions within family–school partnership interventions
examples: Items include "I tell this teacher (parent) when I am concerned" and "I ask this teacher’s (parent’s) opinion about my child’s progress"

Congruence in Parent–Teacher Communication: Implications for the Efficacy of CBC for Students With Behavioral Concerns. article_title: Effects of a Target-Task Problem-Solving Model on Senior Secondary School Students' Performance in Physics
citation: Olaniyan, A. O., & Omosewo, E. O. (2015). Effects of a Target-Task Problem-Solving Model on Senior Secondary School Students' Performance in Physics. Science Education International, 25(4), 522-538.
title: Performance Test on Current Electricity (PTCE)
description: The PTCE is a researcher-designed performance test used as both pre-test and post-test in the study. It "contained 10 items drawn from concepts on current electricity". It was validated and its reliability was established with the Kuder-Richardson KR21 formula, yielding "a coefficient of 0.84". It served to group students into high, medium and low scoring levels and to measure performance change after the six-week intervention.
requirements: Used with lesson notes on the Target-Task Model and Lecture Methods forming the Research Instructional Package
constraints: Covers current electricity concepts only, at senior secondary level
target_learning_goals: current electricity knowledge and problem solving
examples: Administered in week one as pre-test and week six as post-test to both experimental and control groups

article_title: Peer Teaching Experiences of Final Year Paramedic Students: 2011-2012
citation: Williams, Brett; Fellows, Holly; Eastwood, Kathryn, and Wallis, Jaime. (2014). Peer teaching experiences of final year paramedic students: 2011–2012. Journal of Peer Learning, 7, 81-91. http://ro.uow.edu.au/ajpl/vol7/iss1/7
title: Peer Teaching Experience Questionnaire (PTEQ), a 14-item Likert instrument adapted for paramedic students
description: The PTEQ is a 14-statement questionnaire using a 5-point Likert response format, originally developed to evaluate peer learning of first year nursing students and adapted by McKenna and French (2011) for third year nursing students. This study modified it for paramedic students by changing "nursing" to "paramedics" in three items, with no other wording changes, and added an open-ended feedback question. It was completed voluntarily and anonymously by 41 peer teachers after their final tutorial.
requirements: Adaptation to the target student population requires only minimal wording changes to remain valid as described
constraints: The instrument was modified only by changing three items from nursing to paramedic wording
target_learning_goals: evaluating the peer teaching experience
examples: Used at the conclusion of the final tutorial in October 2011 and 2012; questionnaires took approximately 10 minutes to complete.

citation: Olaniyan, Ademola Olatide, Omosewo, Esther O., & Nwankwo, Levi I. (2015). Effect of polya problem-solving model on senior secondary school students' performance in current electricity. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 3(1), 97-104. https://ojcs.siue.edu/ojs/index.php/ejsme
title: Performance Test in Current Electricity (PTCE)
description: The Performance Test in Current Electricity (PTCE) is the instrument used to pre-test and post-test both groups in this study. It was administered as a two-hour test at pre-test, with questions retrieved from students immediately afterwards, and a two-hour post-test was administered in the sixth week. Post-test PTCE scores served as the dependent variable in the ANCOVA analyses, with terminal results used beforehand to group students into three scoring levels.
requirements: Administered as a two-hour test to both experimental and control groups before and after the four-week teaching period
constraints: Used with Senior Secondary School Two physics students in Ilorin metropolis, Kwara State, Nigeria
target_learners: Senior Secondary School Two physics students
target_learning_goals: Current electricity concepts and problem solving in physics
examples: Pre-test and post-test scores fed the ANCOVA comparing Polya and lecture groups

article_title: The role of the 2023 earthquakes in the competencies and critical thinking skills of teacher candidates in Türkiye.
citation: Görgülü Deniz, Cömert Melike, Demir Mustafa, Şahin Çiğdem. (2026). The role of the 2023 earthquakes in the competencies and critical thinking skills of teacher candidates in Türkiye. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05006-2
title: Post-Traumatic Growth theory as a framework for earthquake-exposed teacher candidates' cognitive and professional transformation
description: The article applies Post-Traumatic Growth (PTG) theory, which "posits that individuals who undergo highly challenging life crises can experience positive psychological transformation, encompassing new personal strengths, enriched relationships, and revised life philosophy." The framework explains how the 2023 earthquakes functioned as a context prompting questioning of prior professional assumptions and re-evaluation of pedagogical values. The authors emphasize PTG "is neither automatic nor universal," depending on perceived social support, psychological resilience, and individual coping resources.
requirements: Positive transformation emerges from the cognitive and emotional struggle to rebuild a coherent worldview, not from the traumatic event itself
constraints: The article states the interpretation "is constrained to the specific population and institutional setting examined" and does not imply earthquake exposure universally enhances critical thinking
target_learners: teacher candidates who directly experienced the 2023 earthquakes in Türkiye
target_learning_goals: critical thinking development
professional competency perceptions
key_sources: Görgülü Deniz, Cömert Melike, Demir Mustafa, Şahin Çiğdem. (2026). The role of the 2023 earthquakes in the competencies and critical thinking skills of teacher candidates in Türkiye. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-05006-2

article_title: M(1)ündlich - S(t)imulation of competency-oriented learning in physiology.
citation: Eiring Lisa, Benson Sven, Fandrey Joachim, Prost-Fingerle Katrin, Winning Sandra. (2026). M1ündlich – S(t)imulation of competency-oriented learning in physiology. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09661-2
title: PT-BET (peer teaching-based exam training) program for physiology oral exam preparation
description: PT-BET is a peer-teaching-based exam training program developed at the Institute of Physiology at the University of Duisburg-Essen to prepare third-semester medical students for oral examinations. Students work in groups of five, alternating between teacher and learner roles by asking each other questions randomly drawn from a pre-selected question pool, under the guidance of trained near-peer tutors who completed a structured two-day preparatory training. The program comprises two training rounds (T1 and T2) offered in parallel with the physiology lecture, with each session including extensive structured feedback based on a standardized evaluation form covering structure and density of answers, presentation quality, expression and precision. The program aims to practice the structure, expression, and content depth of oral exams and to gain confidence in dealing with exam situations.
requirements: Trained tutors who completed a structured two-day preparatory training session
A pre-selected question pool
Standardized evaluation forms for feedback
constraints: Has only been used in the preclinical section of medical studies so far
target_learning_goals: Reducing anxiety, stress and blackouts
Improving exam rhetoric and structuring
Encouraging small-group preparation

article_title: Students Perceive Similar Gains in Collaboration, Communication and Professional Skills in Two Distinct Experiential Learning Courses.

Students Perceive Similar Gains in Collaboration, Communication and Professional Skills in Two Distinct Experiential Learning Courses. Pharmacology Research & Perspectives. https://doi.org/10.1002/prp2.70095
title: Pharmacology and Toxicology in Society (PT SOC): a community-engaged experiential learning elective with harm reduction partners
description: PT SOC is an elective enrolling approximately 35 third- and fourth-year students per year in which students "collaborate with harm‐reduction and mental health organizations over one semester." Students work mainly in teams on partner organization-led activities requiring a minimum of 20 hours of work placement outside class time, including community outreach, knowledge translation resources, and community-led research, complemented by course content on drug policy and debates and a community partner panel.
requirements: Students complete a minimum of 20 h of work placement with a community partner organization outside of class time
constraints: It is a partnership-based form of EL whose components occur directly with community partners at community sites, and enrollment is limited to approximately 35 students per year
target_learners: third- and fourth-year undergraduate pharmacology and toxicology students
target_learning_goals: pharmacological and toxicological understanding of substance use disorders
professional and interpersonal skills
communication skills
examples: Students participated in debates on controversial topics in this field and in a community partner panel discussion; top open-ended themes included interpersonal skills (28%), professionalism (24%), and communication skills (17%)

article_title: A randomized controlled trial comparison of PTEBL and traditional teaching methods in "Stop the Bleed" training.
citation: Zhao Wanchen, Cao Yangbo, Hu Liangrong, Lu Chenxiao, Liu Gaoming, Gong Matthew, He Jinshen. (2024). A randomized controlled trial comparison of PTEBL and traditional teaching methods in “Stop the Bleed” training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05457-4
title: PTEBL: problem-, team- and evidence-based learning approach to Stop the Bleed training
description: PTEBL is a three-session teaching approach combining problem-based learning (1.5 h), team-based learning (2 h), and evidence-based learning (0.5 h) within a four-hour Stop the Bleed course. The PBL session poses scenario questions; the TBL session has students practice skills in small teams with role-played scenario simulation and peer critique; the EBL session follows "a) developing an answerable question, b) finding the best available evidence, c) evaluation the evidence and d) applying the evidence to a patient care decision." The article applies it to teach hemostasis skills while explicitly training teamwork.
requirements: A single instructor experienced in educational reform and certified in Stop the Bleed
Small groups in which each student performs at least one tourniquet placement and plays scenario roles
constraints: Teamwork gains may not benefit every STB action, since building a team in real life is difficult and single practice cannot reflect the method's effectiveness
target_learners: Third-year medical students in a five-year training program
target_learning_goals: Hemostasis techniques (direct finger compression, packing, tourniquet placement)
Teamwork and comprehensive emergency response competence
examples: Students read a traumatic-bleeding scenario adapted from a medical TV series and answered four questions about pre-hospital emergency medical services operations
Teams simulated a brachial artery injury after a ground level fall, with members playing the victim, the victim's friend, the primary rescuer, and the rescuer's colleague
key_sources: Zhao Wanchen, Cao Yangbo, Hu Liangrong, Lu Chenxiao, Liu Gaoming, Gong Matthew, He Jinshen. (2024). A randomized controlled trial comparison of PTEBL and traditional teaching methods in “Stop the Bleed” training. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05457-4

article_title: Testing a new active learning approach to advance motor learning knowledge and self-efficacy in physical therapy undergraduate education.
citation: Vaz DV, Ferreira EMR, Palma GB, Atun-Einy O, Kafri M, Ferreira FR. (2021). Testing a new active learning approach to advance motor learning knowledge and self-efficacy in physical therapy undergraduate education. BMC Medical Education 21:62. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02486-1
title: Physical Therapists' Perceptions of Motor Learning (PTP-ML) questionnaire and its adapted Brazilian version
description: A standardized questionnaire with "adequate construct validity, internal consistency, and test-retest reliability" that assesses PTs' self-efficacy, self-reported ML implementation, and environmental workplace factors with three separate scales. The study translated the self-efficacy scale into Portuguese and created an adapted version with Part A (12 original self-efficacy statements) and Part B (8 new statements on the Kleynen framework content), used to map self-efficacy gaps before and after the course.
requirements: Educators can use the self-efficacy scale to map gaps in clinicians' and students' ML self-efficacy before and after educational interventions
constraints: The article states the PTP-ML is a relatively new tool whose relevance to clinical practice has not been researched extensively
target_learning_goals: assessing and facilitating motor learning self-efficacy
examples: Reliability testing in 45 students and 19 professionals yielded ICCs of 0.92 and 0.88 and Cronbach's Alphas of 0.93 and 0.92 for parts A and B
key_sources: Vaz DV, Ferreira EMR, Palma GB, Atun-Einy O, Kafri M, Ferreira FR. (2021). Testing a new active learning approach to advance motor learning knowledge and self-efficacy in physical therapy undergraduate education. BMC Medical Education 21:62. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02486-1

article_title: Developing a programme theory to explain how primary health care teams learn to respond to intimate partner violence: a realist case-study.
citation: Goicolea Isabel, Hurtig Anna-Karin, San Sebastian Miguel, Vives-Cases Carmen, Marchal Bruno. (2015). Developing a programme theory to explain how primary health care teams learn to respond to intimate partner violence: a realist case-study. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-015-0899-8
title: Refined programme theory PT2: IPV policy interventions reach provider groups differently depending on personal motivation
description: PT2 is the refined realist programme theory this article develops to explain how primary health care teams learn to respond to intimate partner violence. It links intervention components (protocols, training, monitoring, IPV coordinators) to mechanisms (legitimisation, recognition, self-efficacy) and outcomes, conditioned on context. The article states the intervention 'is likely to reach different provider groups differently in function of their personal motivation' and that its 'existence in itself (even if weakly implemented) provides legitimacy and an enabling structure for primary health care professionals already responding to IPV'. It specifies enabling contexts: personal ideology (feminism/equality), a woman-centred team approach, a management style valuing team learning, safe reflection spaces, therapeutic groups for women and referral networks.
requirements: Formulated for testing and further refinement in subsequent realist evaluation cycles; built from a prior programme theory (PT1) developed from literature review and planner interviews
constraints: Derived from a single purposively selected exceptional case (La Virgen) and not intended as a final middle-range theory
Does not distinguish implementation failure from policy failure
target_learning_goals: learning to detect and respond to intimate partner violence
team learning on sensitive health issues
examples: The La Virgen case study in Murcia, where the theory's context-mechanism-outcome configurations were identified through interviews, observation, document review and PREMIS questionnaires
key_sources: Goicolea Isabel, Hurtig Anna-Karin, San Sebastian Miguel, Vives-Cases Carmen, Marchal Bruno. (2015). Developing a programme theory to explain how primary health care teams learn to respond to intimate partner violence: a realist case-study. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-015-0899-8
